page.text:
In mathematics, sometimes what looks like an infix operator actually
introduces a new symbol. For example, if $B$ is a set and one says let
$A \subset B$, what they mean is $A$ is a set and is specifically a set
whose elements all are elements of $B$.

Infix Describes allow one to communicate this in Mathlingua:

```mlg
[A \:subset:/ B]
Describes: A
when: B is \set
extends: A is \set
satisfies:
. forAll: X "in" A
  then: X "in"? B
Requires:
. capability: x_ "in" A :-> x_ "in" B
Documented:
. called: "$A?$ is a subset of $B?$"
. written: "A? \subset B?"
Id: "2b2b89a1-d106-4377-ae48-14c704063e5e"
```

A infix describes is of the form `<symbol> \:...:/ <expression>` and the
left hand side of the `\:...:/` must match exactly the symbol introduced
in `Describes: ...`.

Here the `when:` section specifies that the argument `B` must satisfy `B
is \set`. Further, the `extends: A is \set` specifies that by saying `A
\:subset:/ B` one is saying that `A is \set` with additional properties.

Those additional properties are communicated in the `satisfies:` section.
Specifically that $A \subset B$ means every element of $A$ is an element
of $B$.
